title: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia
hook: a leader honored as the king of the community

segments.voice: Yesterday, the scattered bands became the Dal Khalsa, and every chief stepped back a little. Your line was one army. Where did you let the group move together? Today, the man they chose to lead it. Day eight hundred sixty.

A boy is singing in a household in Delhi. His father has died, and his mother has brought him a long way from Punjab, to the home of Mata Sundari, Guru Gobind Singh's widow, the woman whose letters guided the scattered sangats. Tradition says she took the boy in, and that the household got used to hearing him sing the morning hymns. Years later, that boy would ride at the head of the Dal Khalsa, and Sikhs would give him a title that sounds like a crown. Today: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia.
screen: `A FATHERLESS BOY IN DELHI.` → `MATA SUNDARI TAKES HIM IN.` → `HE SINGS THE MORNING HYMNS.`

segments.voice: The title was Sultan-ul-Qaum. Sultan is a king, and qaum is a people, a community, a nation. The king of the community. It's a big name. So it's worth looking at how tradition says he grew into it, because none of it starts with a crown. It starts with a song. In Mata Sundari's house, tradition says, he learned kirtan, singing the Guru's hymns, and he kept singing them all his life. Then he was handed on to Nawab Kapur Singh, who led the Sikh bands. Under him, tradition says, the boy worked: looking after horses, serving in the langar, the free kitchen, doing the jobs nobody writes poems about. Kapur Singh watched him, and in time named him as the one to carry the leadership on. So by the time the gathering at Amritsar chose him to head the Dal Khalsa, he had been formed by two people who led by serving: a widow who kept the community together with letters, and a nawab who fanned the congregation. And that's the shape of leadership Sikhs prize in him. The Sikh scripture is wary of rulers who think power makes them great. Guru Nanak, in a hard line here in paraphrase, compares the kings of his day to tigers and their officials to dogs. Jassa Singh's story is told as the other kind. Notice too that the title is about the qaum, the people, not the land. A sultan of a country owns ground. A leader of the qaum carries people. Sikhs remember him, among other things, as a fighter who stood at the front, and as a man who was, tradition says, still singing the morning hymns. A leader of the qaum.
screen: `SULTAN-UL-QAUM: KING OF THE COMMUNITY.` · `RAISED BY MATA SUNDARI, SINGING KIRTAN.` · `SERVING UNDER NAWAB KAPUR SINGH.` · `A LEADER WHO CARRIES PEOPLE.` · then, large: `LEADER OF THE QAUM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lead by serving. Settle, and breathe slowly. Think of somewhere you have a little say, even a small one: a family dinner, a project, a friend group, a shift at work. Picture the people there. Now ask: what's the job nobody wants, the horse nobody grooms, the dish nobody washes? Let one come to mind. See yourself doing it, quietly, before anyone asks. Notice how that changes the way you'd speak to the group afterward. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Jassa Singh. Raised, tradition says, in Mata Sundari's household and trained by Nawab Kapur Singh, he led the Dal Khalsa and was honored as Sultan-ul-Qaum, king of the community. Today's word.
Your line: leader of the qaum. Today, wherever you have any say at all, do the unglamorous job first, then speak. Day eight hundred sixty.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Jassa Singh Ahluwalia as Sultan-ul-Qaum, and his story is told in gurdwara talks and Sikh history lessons as an example of a leader formed by kirtan and seva.

original.note: Gurmukhi spelling of the Persian title Sultan-ul-Qaum, king of the community, given to Jassa Singh Ahluwalia.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jassa Singh Ahluwalia was a warlord with a royal title.
what it means: tradition remembers a boy raised on kirtan in Mata Sundari's house and trained by serving under Nawab Kapur Singh.
what a scholar hears: his title names the qaum, the people, not a territory, and Sikh tradition tells his rise as leadership through seva.

notes: His upbringing in Mata Sundari's household in Delhi, his kirtan (tradition often says Asa di Var), and his service under Nawab Kapur Singh with horses and langar follow the common telling; confirm.

The paraphrased line of Guru Nanak ('kings are tigers', Var Malar, Ang 1288: 'raje sheeh mukadam kute') is paraphrased as comparing kings to tigers and officials to dogs; confirm the Ang and the paraphrase.
Sultan-ul-Qaum: Gurmukhi spelling ਸੁਲਤਾਨ-ਉਲ-ਕੌਮ and pronunciation; confirm.
No dates or ages given for his time with Mata Sundari or his appointment; confirm.
